rows.statement: Recent community reports describe four to five hours of preparation for a three-hour session, extensive context switching, and repeated frustration when carefully prepared material is ignored. These are anecdotal buyer-pain signals, not conversion rates.

rows.title: Current premium and free prep suites close the broad GM-prep category
rows.statement: SessionFlow, World & Campaign Builder, RPGM Forge, current AI/prep tools, and Foundry premium content occupy campaign planning, live widgets, player panels, content generation, or ready-made preparation.

rows.title: A new prep product would need safe reuse of discarded preparation rather than another workspace
rows.statement: The remaining narrow hypothesis is to recover unused scenes, NPCs, promises, or encounters when players pivot, while preserving permissions, provenance, and publisher-content boundaries. More canvas or generated content is not enough.

rows.title: Player Compass remains the first empirical gate after the recurring-prep scan
rows.statement: Player Compass combines recurring use with a visible premium UX category, while BridgeCheck retains migration urgency and World Doctor retains long-running incident value. No candidate has product-specific WTP yet.

rows.title: Generic prep workspace, generic AI prep, and generic session scheduling remain negative controls
rows.statement: Fresh prep pain does not justify opening another broad product because exact current tools and free alternatives remain strong. Reopen only for a named pivot or prep-loss failure with non-zero price evidence.

rows.title: Player Compass must use separate system adapters and a neutral capability manifest
rows.statement: D&D5e and PF2e expose different action semantics, permissions, sheet controls, and content surfaces. A safe product asks each system adapter what it can describe instead of becoming a universal rules engine.

rows.title: Foundry Navigator, Token Action HUD D&D5e, and PF2e HUD close the broad action-access promise
rows.statement: Foundry Navigator covers keyboard and screen-reader navigation plus target, damage, healing, focus, and low-resolution workflows; Token Action HUD provides direct D&D5e rolls and item use; PF2e HUD is current for PF2e and Starfinder 2e.

rows.title: The remaining Player Compass wedge is zero-setup, read-only context explanation
rows.statement: The product must explain what is relevant now and why, preserve the native sheet and exact HUD stack, and keep every action user-invoked without hidden writes or a replacement rules engine.

rows.title: Player Compass must read user-owned data and audit system/package rights
rows.statement: The D&D5e repository separates MIT software from SRD and asset terms, while PF2e separates Apache-2.0 code from content, art, and Foundry platform terms. These are audit inputs, not permission to copy rules text, compendium data, publisher art, or competitor code.

rows.title: Player Compass portability is limited to a capability-manifest and intent contract
rows.statement: Capability IDs, labels, context, visibility, prerequisites, provenance, and user-invoked intent can be mapped to another browser VTT; actual action semantics, permission checks, and accessibility behavior remain system/VTT-specific.

rows.title: Accessibility and context claims require real fixture evidence
rows.statement: Keyboard order, screen-reader labels, low-resolution layout, focus recovery, reconnect, per-user visibility, and deterministic context transitions must be tested with synthetic D&D5e and PF2e actors rather than inferred from package descriptions.

rows.title: Player Compass remains the first empirical gate but is not selected
rows.statement: The technical boundary is now narrower and safer, but exact-HUD preference, a non-zero price, three-session use, rights clearance, and a second-VTT manifest proof remain outstanding.

rows.title: Foundry version fragmentation is a recurring consumer-GM pain signal
rows.statement: A recent high-engagement discussion describes breaking API changes, delayed system/module updates, uncertainty around paid content, multiple parallel versions, refusal to upgrade, and users leaving or avoiding purchases. This is recruiting evidence, not conversion data.

rows.title: Campaign Anchor / Version Harbor is a fresh consumer-GM challenger
rows.statement: A local-first manager could pin each campaign's Foundry/system/module environment, clone before upgrade, rehearse on a disposable copy, preserve a known-good launch, and provide deterministic rollback without touching the live world.

rows.title: Foundry portable installs and managed hosts close the broad Campaign Anchor promise
rows.statement: Foundry officially supports older versions, Windows portable builds, independent User Data folders, and simultaneous versions; The Forge supports different Foundry versions per game; Molten offers managed hosting and backups; current modules cover diagnosis and package control.

rows.title: The Campaign Anchor wedge is a campaign-specific environment lock and play-tonight receipt
rows.statement: Version lists, compatibility badges, backups, and another launcher are not enough. The product must answer what changed, whether the live world is untouched, and which known-good environment will launch now.

rows.title: Campaign Anchor payer is a self-hosting GM with a long-running or paid campaign
rows.statement: One-shot GMs and managed-host users are negative controls; the strongest payer hypothesis has premium content, multiple worlds, a large module stack, or a recent upgrade near-miss.

rows.title: Campaign Anchor portability is weak and should begin Foundry-only
rows.statement: The lockfile idea can later map to another self-hosted VTT, but world migration, package manifests, server launch, license rules, and rollback semantics are platform-specific.

rows.title: Campaign Anchor must never bundle licensed binaries or mutate the known-good world silently
rows.statement: The first slice should use user-installed Foundry and packages, explicit paths, copy-on-write rehearsal, visible backups, and user-authorized launch; it must not bypass license checks or upload worlds.

rows.title: Foundry core already covers much of Campaign Anchor's backup and restore promise
rows.statement: Current Foundry supports package backups, full snapshots, automatic pre-migration backup, package or snapshot restore, notes, storage metadata, and compatibility-risk information.

rows.title: Foundry portable installs already cover version pinning and multiple local versions
rows.statement: Official guidance supports older versions, Windows portable builds, separate User Data folders, and simultaneous installations with separate ports.

rows.title: Document-level backup and managed hosting further narrow Campaign Anchor
rows.statement: Sephral's Content Backup & Restore covers named document recovery; The Forge and Molten provide managed version or backup alternatives.

rows.title: The only remaining Campaign Anchor wedge is a campaign-specific environment receipt
rows.statement: A receipt must combine world, core, system, module, launch-path, and rehearsal state and answer whether the known-good world is runnable; a backup, version list, or launcher alone is not enough.

rows.title: Campaign Anchor lacks product-specific WTP after the core-coverage correction
rows.statement: Version anxiety is strong recruiting evidence, but included Foundry backups and paid hosting substitutes do not prove that a self-hosting GM will buy another local utility.

rows.title: Campaign Anchor portability is a reusable protocol asset, not a launch promise
rows.statement: Environment lock and rollback semantics depend on Foundry world format, package manifests, migration behavior, and server launch model; a second VTT requires separate proof.

rows.title: Between-session project engagement is a recurring D&D5e 2024 recruiting signal
rows.statement: Bastions, crafting, research, orders, and other downtime projects give players reasons to engage between weekly or biweekly sessions, but interest in official content is not utility WTP.

rows.title: Between Sessions / Campaign Projects is a player-first asynchronous workflow hypothesis
rows.statement: A GM-authored station and project board could collect player actions, costs, checks, collaborators, approvals, deadlines, and results, then produce a next-session receipt without a Discord spreadsheet.

rows.title: The current downtime and Bastion package category is highly occupied
rows.statement: Indy Ventures, Downtime 5e, Downtime Manager, Yugen Downtime, Universal Downtime Engine, Morelord Downtime, the official D&D5e Bastion UI, and shared spreadsheets cover broad projects, progress, checks, rewards, crafting, research, and venture workflows.

rows.title: The likely Between Sessions payer is a weekly or biweekly D&D5e 2024 GM
rows.statement: Paid GMs and groups already using Bastions or downtime are the strongest segment; one-shots and campaigns that do not use between-session projects are negative controls.

rows.title: Any remaining wedge is approval and reconciliation workflow, not another downtime tracker
rows.statement: A new product would need player-first submission, GM batch approval, clear deadlines, conflict handling, auditable receipts, and provenance while preserving GM authority and avoiding silent actor, item, or currency writes.

rows.title: Project-state portability is plausible only as a neutral contract
rows.statement: Project IDs, status, participant, costs, deadlines, approvals, provenance, and results can be represented neutrally, while checks, currency, item automation, and bastion semantics require VTT/system adapters.

rows.title: Between Sessions remains parked without product-specific WTP
rows.statement: Official D&D5e content and active modules establish category demand, but no evidence yet shows that a new approval/reconciliation utility beats the exact package set and a shared spreadsheet at a non-zero price.

rows.title: Session-zero expectation mismatch is a recurring campaign risk
rows.statement: Recent discussions repeatedly identify tone, boundaries, house rules, communication, attendance, and campaign buy-in as topics that need explicit alignment before or during a campaign; failure can contribute to group collapse, but this is not product-specific WTP.

rows.title: Table Pact is a privacy-preserving versioned agreement hypothesis
rows.statement: A Foundry-first flow could collect private player preferences, expose only aggregate conflicts and unanswered items to the GM, record acknowledgements, and support re-checks when the campaign changes.

rows.title: Current safety modules and ordinary communication are strong controls
rows.statement: Safety Tools, Safety and Communication, Consent Form, shared checklists/forms, and direct conversation cover much of session-zero and safety workflow; no broad gap should be claimed without exact-table comparison.

rows.title: The strongest Table Pact payer segment is new, paid, convention, or organized-play tables
rows.statement: Established friend groups are a negative control because they may already know their boundaries; the strongest test cohort has a named mismatch or a high cost of onboarding strangers.

rows.title: A portable pact must exclude raw sensitive answers
rows.statement: A neutral second-VTT artifact can carry consent-safe categories, pact version, acknowledgements, and aggregate unresolved flags, but it must not export private responses or interpersonal judgments.

rows.title: Table Pact has no product-specific WTP yet
rows.statement: A non-zero $5/$10/$20 choice and pilot completion are required; session-zero participation, safety-tool adoption, or high-vote community discussion cannot be treated as payment evidence.

rows.title: Mundane resource bookkeeping is a recurring friction but often an opt-out choice
rows.statement: Recent discussions describe ammunition tracking as cumbersome and often ignored or hand-waved; the pain is strongest in survival, expedition, firearms, or resource-management campaigns rather than ordinary high-fantasy tables.

rows.title: Current Foundry resource tools cover most broad ammunition and counter automation
rows.statement: Ammo Tracker, RC Spent, Weapon Reload, Party Resources, Custom Fields, and Bag o' Lists cover ammunition use/recovery, reload/loadout, shared counters, item counters, or custom resources.

rows.title: The plausible Resource Steward payer is a resource-focused GM
rows.statement: Survival, expedition, firearms, and paid GMs who intentionally enforce supply rules are the only qualified segment; ordinary tables that hand-wave the resource are negative controls.

rows.title: Resource-event portability is plausible but resolution semantics need adapters
rows.statement: Consume, recover, lose, reserve, threshold, and receipt events can be neutral, while encumbrance, ammunition recovery, firearms, and survival rules require system adapters or user-authored policy.

rows.title: Resource Steward is not a broad market candidate without narrow non-zero WTP
rows.statement: A native item quantity, macro, existing module, or a decision to ignore mundane bookkeeping is a stronger substitute for most groups; test only qualified resource-focused buyers.

rows.title: Long-running, open, paid, and always-on worlds can need character-change provenance
rows.statement: GMs may need to identify unexplained item, stat, spell-slot, or biography changes between sessions, but the incident rate and payment need are not established for ordinary private groups.

rows.title: Character Tracker and yugen-tracker already cover the broad character audit value
rows.statement: Character Tracker provides actor/core-data, embedded-item, active-effect, chronological, categorical, and export views; yugen-tracker provides real-time tracking, alerts, history, optional file output, player visibility, and Discord delivery.

rows.title: Character Integrity Ledger has a narrow payer segment
rows.statement: Paid GMs, organized/open tables, and worlds intentionally available between sessions are the strongest segment; normal private friend groups are a negative control.

rows.title: Character audit logs can create material trust and privacy risk
rows.statement: Biography changes, player behavior, GM corrections, and rollback actions require role filtering, retention controls, explicit acknowledgement, and no person-level suspicion or public accusation surface.

rows.title: A redacted character-change contract is portable but raw data is not
rows.statement: Redacted events, actor/item identifiers, timestamps, provenance, and acknowledgement state can be represented neutrally; raw character data, private biography, and person-level suspicion must remain in-world.

rows.title: Character Integrity Ledger is rejected as a broad new product
rows.statement: The general audit value is already available in current Foundry modules and no product-specific WTP or unmet incident rate is established; only a narrow unexplained-incident wedge remains testable.

rows.title: Reusable integrity assets are immutable change events and reversible receipts
rows.statement: Retain role-filtered views, retention controls, explicit revert previews, and no-accusation UX without turning a trust tool into surveillance or silently rolling back legitimate play.

rows.title: Hybrid and in-person Foundry groups lack a supported mobile player surface
rows.statement: Foundry core does not support mobile devices, while current groups report laptop clutter, tablet-only players, and a need for sheet-only or native mobile access during in-person play.

rows.title: The Player Pocket payer is the GM of a hybrid or tablet-constrained table
rows.statement: The GM controls the Foundry world and can pay once for free player invites; desktop-only online groups and unsupported systems are negative controls.

rows.title: The broad Foundry mobile companion category is crowded and active
rows.statement: Foundry Tabletop Helpers, Swipe VTT, VTT Companion, PocketScroll, Diecast, Sheet Only, Mobile Improvements, and system-specific Mobile-Companion modules cover mobile sheets, rolls, HP, inventory, combat, maps, or offline access.

rows.title: Current mobile competitors provide a genuine payment proxy
rows.statement: PocketScroll and VTT Companion use GM-paid access with free player invites, and both expose one-time/lifetime options alongside or instead of subscriptions; this validates category payment, not new-product WTP.

rows.title: The only defensible Player Pocket wedge is a portable player-action contract
rows.statement: A narrow contract can carry permission-scoped character snapshot, action request, roll/result, resource delta, combat notification, reconnect, and read-only offline cache without recreating the canvas or copying rules text.

rows.title: Player Pocket has material sync, auth, adapter, and version-drift risk
rows.statement: A Foundry bridge must respect actor/document permissions, reconnects, offline conflicts, system-specific sheets, app-store constraints, and Foundry-version changes; static package descriptions do not prove reliability.

rows.title: Player-action portability is plausible only at a normalized event boundary
rows.statement: A second-VTT adapter can map snapshots, permitted actions, results, resource deltas, and notifications, while full sheets, rules semantics, canvas operations, and private raw data remain platform-specific.

rows.title: Player Pocket is conditional and not yet selected
rows.statement: The category has strong pain and payment signals, but current competitors already deliver the obvious mobile demo; exact-alternative preference, one-time WTP, multi-session sync, and privacy evidence are still missing.

rows.title: PocketScroll already covers the broad current Foundry mobile bridge
rows.statement: PocketScroll uses Foundry Socket.IO and provides current D&D5e player sheets, actions, rolls, inventory, rests, combat, maps, chat, journals, GM controls, and live two-way synchronization on supported Foundry versions.

rows.title: Swipe VTT and VTT Companion cover current mobile sheet and action gaps
rows.statement: Swipe is current on Foundry v14.367 with touch, performance, D&D5e/Daggerheart sheets, chat, inventory, spells, combat, and Midi-QoL integration; VTT Companion separates a free bridge from premium two-way updates for D&D5e v13/v14.

rows.title: Roll20 Characters and D&D Beyond are strong cross-platform mobile substitutes
rows.statement: Roll20 documents mobile browser character sheets with D&D5e phone/tablet support and VTT synchronization, while D&D Beyond provides mobile/offline sheets, rolls, spells, inventory, and character access.

rows.title: Player Pocket should be demoted to a conditional comparison arm
rows.statement: A new multi-VTT adapter has no demonstrated WTP and would inherit per-VTT authentication, data-model, system, app-store, and maintenance costs; reopen only for a named cross-VTT failure and two-VTT pilot.

rows.title: Recurring GMs report encounter-fit and preparation friction
rows.statement: Recent community discussions describe substantial session preparation and encounters that land too easy or too hard for the actual roster; this recruits qualified buyers but does not establish product-specific payment.

rows.title: Encounter Forge already calibrates generated creatures to a party
rows.statement: Current Encounter Forge estimates or reads party HP, AC, saves, levels, DPR, difficulty, enemy count, and solo-boss settings, then tunes generated creatures to an encounter envelope on Foundry v12-v14.

rows.title: Monster Maker and D&D Beyond occupy the broad builder promise
rows.statement: Giffyglyph's current Monster Maker continuation provides level scaling, combat roles, scaling actions, and conversion of existing monsters, while D&D Beyond's Encounter Builder is subscriber-gated and supplies party setup, filters, drag-and-drop monsters, and difficulty math.

rows.title: Current analytics tools already record substantial combat history
rows.statement: Combat Stats, Battle Replay, and Encounter Stats cover combinations of damage, healing, kills, downed events, rounds, accuracy, resources, replay, charts, exports, and encounter reports; PF2e has additional danger and simulation tools.

rows.title: Encounter Tuner must be post-combat feedback, not another generator
rows.statement: The only defensible wedge is a transparent planned-versus-observed debrief followed by small, reversible, GM-approved next-encounter adjustments; live hidden scaling, actor rewrites, proprietary rules text, and opaque balance scores are out of scope.

rows.title: Encounter Tuner's payer is a recurring combat-heavy GM
rows.statement: One-shot-only, story-first, and already-satisfied tables are negative controls; test the GM with a $10/$20/$35/no-purchase one-time offer and require three-session use.

rows.title: Encounter Tuner can carry a neutral combat-event contract
rows.statement: Encounter identity, rounds, actor roles, outcome metrics, resource deltas, and GM-authored notes can be portable; damage semantics, hidden stats, automation hooks, and live mutations remain adapter-specific.

rows.title: Encounter Tuner is conditional and not selected
rows.statement: Current generators and analytics may already close the need; exact-alternative preference, non-zero WTP, three-session use, and runtime/privacy evidence are missing.

rows.title: Map import and scene preparation have strong current substitutes
rows.statement: Universal Battlemap Importer handles current Dungeondraft, DungeonFog, and Arkenforge exports; Dungeon Alchemist, Dungeondraft, MapForge, Mass Import, its level importer, and Map Splitter cover creation, import, levels, and scene organization.

rows.title: Map software payment does not transfer to a map QA utility
rows.statement: Dungeon Alchemist advertises a $44.99 one-time purchase and Dungeondraft advertises a one-time no-subscription model; those are payment anchors for creation, not proof for a second post-import validator.

rows.title: SceneReady would overlap BridgeCheck and World Doctor
rows.statement: The remaining map QA wedge is visual grid/wall/door/light/level validation, missing-file detection, before-after diff, and a neutral receipt; that is closer to migration and creator packaging assurance than a broad consumer product.

rows.title: SceneReady should be rejected as a standalone product for now
rows.statement: Reopen only for a named repeated post-import failure that survives the exact importer and yields a non-zero price choice; retain readiness receipts, diffs, missing-asset reports, and neutral scene contracts as reusable assets.

rows.title: Some Foundry groups lose a player to device or browser incompatibility
rows.statement: Foundry's current client requirements call for a relatively modern operating system and browser, hardware acceleration, 8 GB of RAM, and a 1366x768 display; the official FAQ also says iPad is not supported because of Safari/WebKit limitations.

rows.title: Recent community reports describe blocked-player incidents
rows.statement: A recent Foundry report describes an older Mac that cannot reach the game and a group considering screen sharing or leaving Foundry; other current discussions describe low-end and mobile constraints, but they do not establish a market size.

rows.title: Performance Optimizer already addresses low-frame-rate clients
rows.statement: Performance Optimizer offers per-player low/medium/high profiles, GM remote controls, low-FPS detection, a benchmark scene, and live player performance monitoring.

rows.title: Current mobile and companion clients cover much of the broad fallback promise
rows.statement: Swipe provides a mobile-friendly interface and performance enhancements, while foundry-mobile-companion provides a portrait-first mobile player interface for D&D5e; the existing mobile category is therefore not open.

rows.title: Foundry Lightweight Client is a current focused client substitute
rows.statement: Foundry Lightweight Client is a bloat-free desktop client for connecting to local, VPN, HTTP, HTTPS, and hosted Foundry servers; it can solve some browser overhead but does not prove support for unsupported browsers or WebGL-limited devices.

rows.title: CanvasBridge must be a canvasless fallback, not a second full VTT
rows.statement: The only defensible wedge is a GM-run fallback surface for a named excluded player: permission-scoped character snapshot, chat, permitted roll/action request, visible result, resource delta, lightweight scene snapshot, reconnect, and explicit unsupported state.

rows.title: CanvasBridge's payer is a GM with a blocked player, not every mobile user
rows.statement: The strongest buyer is a GM/host with a named player who cannot join because of device/browser limitations, especially in a recurring, hybrid, paid, or organized-play table; ordinary mobile convenience users are a negative control.

rows.title: CanvasBridge requires direct one-time WTP evidence
rows.statement: Test $15, $25, and $39 against no purchase for a one-time host license with free player access; free performance settings, FLC, screen sharing, or changing VTT may make the buyer unwilling to pay.

rows.title: CanvasBridge portability belongs at a neutral player-session contract
rows.statement: Visible scene references or snapshots, permitted action requests, results, resource deltas, reconnect state, and unsupported capabilities can be portable; live sheets, canvas operations, hidden data, rules semantics, and authentication remain adapter-specific.

rows.title: CanvasBridge is conditional and not selected
rows.statement: The device-exclusion incident is high urgency for affected groups but episodic and technically expensive; exact-alternative preference, non-zero WTP, two-session retention, and runtime permission evidence are missing.

rows.title: Current D&D5e Mobile Companion covers a substantial player fallback surface
rows.statement: The current Mobile Companion is verified for Foundry 14.365 and exposes health, hit dice, exhaustion, inventory, spells, traits, and a trade app; it is intentionally lighter than a full character-management client and has limited Safari/WebKit support.

rows.title: Companion Bridge and VTT Companion already provide app synchronization and two-way updates
rows.statement: Companion Bridge Free is verified for Foundry 13â€“14.999 and connects to the VTT Companion iOS app; the premium path advertises two-way updates such as HP, item use, and spell use.

rows.title: Foundry Mobile Companion provides a touch player surface with chat and rolls
rows.statement: The current Foundry Mobile Companion supports portrait-first touch sheets, item/spell/feature details, chat messages, a mobile dice widget, and supported D&D5e roll-card actions.

rows.title: The broad CanvasBridge fallback overlaps current client and companion alternatives
rows.statement: Performance profiles, lightweight clients, mobile modules, native companion apps, and screen sharing address different parts of the excluded-player scenario; a new product cannot claim an open general mobile or low-end market.

rows.title: Only a residual unsupported-device case remains testable
rows.statement: The remaining hypothesis requires a named player who cannot use the exact mobile companion, lightweight client, performance profile, or screen-share workaround and would otherwise be excluded or force a VTT migration.

rows.title: CanvasBridge should be demoted to a negative control
rows.statement: Current competitors close the ordinary fallback job; the residual case has no product-specific WTP, repeat frequency, or verified technical path. Retain only the permission and player-session contracts as reusable assets.

rows.title: Players and GMs have asked for named prepared-spell loadouts
rows.statement: Community requests describe situation-specific prepared spell sets such as exploration, dungeon, and combat loadouts; a recent PF2e release reports the same save/apply demand. This is a real workflow signal, not product-specific willingness to pay.

rows.title: D&D5e Spell Book already provides named spell loadouts
rows.statement: Spell Book is verified for Foundry 14 and supports per-class named preparation sets, apply and quick-apply behavior, 2014 and 2024 rules, filters, and player spell management.

rows.title: PF2e Prepper already provides save/apply prepared-spell setups
rows.statement: PF2e Prepper saves and applies prepared spell setups, supports prepared and flexible casters, and has Dailies integration according to its current community release discussion.

rows.title: Native and cross-VTT sheets cover adjacent character state
rows.statement: D&D Beyond and Roll20 provide native spell preparation and equipment management, while Foundry system and equipment tools cover portions of equipped state; this blocks a broad claim that players lack character configuration controls everywhere.

rows.title: Loadout frequency is not universal
rows.statement: Community discussion includes the view that many players do not swap prepared spells often enough to need a dedicated tool, so the payer segment would need repeated non-spell kit changes rather than general interest in presets.

rows.title: The generic Loadout Compass should be rejected
rows.statement: Current spell-loadout tools close the sharpest player request and no product-specific WTP or full-character-state gap has been demonstrated. Retain only a reversible explicit kit record as reusable infrastructure.

rows.title: A current community request identifies repetitive GM damage application as a session-time loss
rows.statement: A recent high-engagement Foundry discussion asks for a GM-controlled trust toggle so players can apply damage to enemy tokens without receiving unrestricted ownership; this is a concrete ordinary-combat friction signal.

rows.title: Effective Tray NG already supports GM-mediated unowned damage and effects
rows.statement: Effective Tray NG is verified for Foundry 13 to 14 and can allow players to apply damage or effects to targets they do not own when the GM enables the relevant settings; unowned updates are routed through an active GM client.

rows.title: Midi-QoL and Damage Application cover much of the D&D5e damage handoff
rows.statement: Midi-QoL can automatically apply damage while Damage Application adds faster damage, healing, temporary-hit-point, and resistance-aware workflows; the broad D&D5e click-saving promise is therefore occupied.

rows.title: Always HP and current D&D5e prompts cover manual or GM-confirmed HP changes
rows.statement: Always HP provides a current v14 HP adjustment window, while current D&D5e tweak packages provide GM/player damage prompts and apply buttons. These are not a general trust layer but are direct substitutes for the motivating task.

rows.title: Delegated actions create a high permission and rules-safety burden
rows.statement: A general player action gateway must distinguish target selection from mutation, preserve hidden state, reject stale and duplicate requests, handle reconnects, and respect system-specific damage and effect semantics without granting NPC ownership.

rows.title: The broad Trusted Table product should be rejected
rows.statement: Exact D&D5e modules cover most of the motivating workflow, while the remaining cross-system version has no product-specific WTP. Retain only neutral whitelist, expiry, audit, and undo concepts as reusable protocol assets.

rows.title: A 2026 community thread gives explicit payment language for a live drawing layer
rows.statement: A recent high-engagement Foundry request says the author would pay real money for an Excalidraw-like layer and separately asks for better text/drawing controls; this is stronger behavioral payment evidence than a generic feature wish.

rows.title: Whiteboard Experience covers much of the collaborative canvas concept but is version-limited
rows.statement: Whiteboard Experience provides collaborative text, shapes, freehand drawing, image paste, multiplayer sync, and freeze controls, but its current package page reports Foundry 11 to 13 support and alpha limitations.

rows.title: Current drawing editors and premium direction occupy the broad drawing category
rows.statement: Foundry core, Advanced Drawing Tools, Dungeon Draw, Gambit's Image Viewer, and Gambit's previewed Enhanced Drawing cover native drawing, richer editing, dungeon mapping, image annotation, or premium canvas improvements.

rows.title: Only a narrow live-play annotation wedge remains plausible
rows.statement: Temporary scene or handout layers, inline text, touch/pen speed, permission scopes, automatic cleanup, and reversible promotion are more specific than a generic whiteboard or map editor, but still require direct buyer comparison.

rows.title: The fresh search did not produce a new selected product
rows.statement: The strongest new evidence refines the existing conditional Tactical Sketchbook candidate rather than opening a distinct winner. Player Compass remains the first recurring-use buyer gate; implementation remains paused.

rows.title: Current Foundry Navigator materially closes the broad player-guidance and delegated-action promise
rows.statement: Foundry Navigator is verified for Foundry 13 to 14 and currently describes per-player setup, keyboard and screen-reader navigation, combat targeting, attack/use/roll flows, GM-mediated damage and healing against unowned hostile tokens, spoken announcements, focus recovery, and low-resolution behavior.

rows.title: Native and current Character Builder onboarding close a generic teach-players module
rows.statement: D&D5e Character Builder includes player tutorials for assigned characters, pending level-ups, rests, and wizard spellbook workflows, while Foundry's official Player Orientation covers joining, claiming a character, character sheets, and map movement.

rows.title: Current performance and mobile packages occupy the weak-client branch
rows.statement: Prime Performance is verified for Foundry 14 and optimizes token/status-effect rendering; Geano's Scene Optimizer provides non-destructive image/audio optimization with progress feedback; Swipe VTT adds touch, mobile sheets, and performance adjustments.

rows.title: The residual Player Compass and performance opportunities are incident-specific
rows.statement: A surviving offer must identify a named failure that survives the exact Navigator, Character Builder, native/HUD, performance, or mobile stack; a new generic HUD, onboarding wizard, FPS dashboard, or low-spec mode is not differentiated.

rows.title: Fresh Pass 128 selected no new product
rows.statement: The current package audit demotes broad player guidance, onboarding, mobile, and performance claims. Player Compass, Session Health Autopsy, and CanvasBridge remain conditional evidence arms only; DMF remains backburnered.

rows.title: Hybrid Foundry tables have a current shared-display workflow demand signal
rows.statement: A current in-person/hybrid discussion describes a GM-controlled Foundry client plus a shared TV/player display, table account, second screen, or combat-only setup; this is buyer-pain evidence, not payment evidence.

rows.title: Current v14 packages occupy the shared-TV and spectator-stage category
rows.statement: Monk's Common Display provides a clean common display and GM-controlled focus for Foundry 14; paid Stage Master provides spectator display, camera cloning, shared vision, player UI control, highlights, media sharing, and a quick curtain.

rows.title: In-person player companion patterns are already available
rows.statement: Sheet Only provides v14 player character-sheet clients, while Physical Play Dice targets in-person sessions with a shared TV/monitor/projector and physical-roll interception. These close generic hybrid companion claims.

rows.title: A current GM scratchpad request is resolved by an existing v14 module
rows.statement: A recent request for a lightweight sidebar note surface was resolved by Notebook, whose current v14 page lists text, list, counter, timer, progress-clock, chat, macro, and scribble notes; GM Screen, Campaign Codex, pinned chat, and map notes are additional substitutes.

rows.title: Fresh Pass 129 selected no new product
rows.statement: Hybrid display control and GM scratchpad are occupied categories. Only a residual cross-VTT private/shared routing and stale-client handoff could reopen Tabletop Bridge, and it still requires named failures, product-specific WTP, and pilots.

rows.title: Live broadcast overlays have explicit creator payment intent
rows.statement: A current community discussion about a polished D&D stream says the author would pay good money for live character portraits, hit points, spell slots, and turn-driven presentation. This is creator/actual-play payment evidence, not ordinary-table WTP.

rows.title: Foundry Stream Overlay Free and Pro occupy live actor overlay layouts
rows.statement: Foundry Stream Overlay is verified for Foundry 12 to 14, supports multiple systems and live customizable actor data, and advertises Pro layouts, animations, slideshows, and transitions.

rows.title: OBS Utils occupies spectator and OBS-control workflows
rows.statement: OBS Utils is current for Foundry 13 to 14 and provides browser-source spectator behavior, token following, viewport tracking, transparent stream mode, custom overlays, and remote OBS control.

rows.title: Broadcast overlays require consent-safe read-only visibility boundaries
rows.statement: A broadcast adapter must prevent hidden HP, private notes, unreleased portraits, and player data from leaking while respecting user-owned assets, permissions, and system-specific actor paths.

rows.title: Fresh Pass 130 rejects a generic broadcast-overlay product for ordinary tables
rows.statement: The category has current free/premium incumbents and the strongest payment signal belongs to streamers or paid actual-play creators. Retain only neutral broadcast packets and consent policy assets; no ordinary-table product was selected.

rows.title: Time-poor Foundry GMs request zero-prep and minimum-configuration workflows
rows.statement: A current community thread includes a request for more zero-prep modules with minimal configuration because Foundry feels complicated and time-consuming. This is a recurring-pain recruiting signal, not observed willingness to pay.

rows.title: Dungeon Flow already sells a broad ready-to-import dungeon workflow
rows.statement: Dungeon Flow supports Foundry 13 and 14 and generates maps, room descriptions, encounters, traps, treasure, GM notes, walls, doors, line of sight, and pinned journals, with import and re-import through its Pro tier.

rows.title: Current encounter and batch-import tools cover major capsule components
rows.statement: Morelord Encounters generates a ready-to-review D&D5e roster from party, difficulty, and available monster sources; Encounter Forge builds party-sized NPCs; Mass Import creates scenes, journals, decks, and other entities from folders.

rows.title: The only plausible Zero-Prep Session Capsule wedge is orchestration of user-owned material
rows.statement: A capsule could preview selected references, enforce player-safe scope, produce a time-boxed runbook, launch a reversible session surface, and emit cleanup/unsupported receipts without bundling rules, adventure text, or protected art.

rows.title: Zero-Prep Session Capsule is a conditional low-priority challenger, not a selected product
rows.statement: The concept may be a convenience bundle over Dungeon Flow, Morelord, Encounter Forge, Mass Import, Adventure Navigator, TableStart, and Rapid Encounter Board. It advances only through exact buyer preference, non-zero WTP, pilots, runtime, rights, and second-VTT evidence.

rows.title: SessionFlow occupies the broad Zero-Prep Session Capsule workspace claim
rows.statement: SessionFlow is verified for Foundry 14 and currently provides a premium one-canvas session workspace with beats, scenes, quick scenes, journal links, checklists, player panels, objectives, live broadcasts, and Scribe recaps.

rows.title: Paid content and import alternatives absorb much of the zero-prep payment path
rows.statement: Dungeon Flow sells paid Foundry import/re-import with walls, doors, line of sight, and room journals, while One-shot Dungeons for 5E sells ready-to-use adventure content. Category payment does not transfer to an orchestration wrapper.

rows.title: Broad Zero-Prep Session Capsule is demoted to a comparison arm
rows.statement: Only a disposable, player-safe transaction wrapper remains distinct: dependency preview, scope review, reversible launch, cleanup, and return receipt. It has no product-specific payment evidence and may be absorbed by incumbents or duplicate-world practice.

rows.title: Monthly and irregular campaigns have a recurring absent-player and lore-recall problem
rows.statement: A current Foundry discussion describes a monthly homebrew campaign whose lore is no longer fresh for players; another describes cancelled sessions, one-shots, duplicated characters, and state-management concerns when a player is absent. This is recruiting evidence, not observed WTP.

rows.title: Recap, wiki, assistant, and map substitutes already cover broad catch-up claims
rows.statement: Archivist Sync provides recaps, linked entities, a campaign chatbot, and bidirectional sync; Foundry Familiar offers campaign Q&A and summaries; Campaign Codex provides linked journals, timelines, and permissions; SessionFlow provides Chronicle and Scribe; LegendKeeper is an external wiki alternative; Foundry shared fog addresses explored geography.

rows.title: No-Spoiler Player Return Brief has a narrow semantic wedge
rows.statement: A GM-approved per-player card can present only allowed facts, session changes, objectives, character state, unresolved hooks, and a safe re-entry point, with redaction, contradiction, revocation, and acknowledgement. It must not become a generic wiki, transcript, search box, or chatbot.

rows.title: Return Brief portability requires a neutral permissioned manifest
rows.statement: The portable artifact can carry source references, audience, spoiler scope, timestamps, confidence, redactions, and acknowledgements. Foundry is first; Roll20 or Owlbear begins as a read-only preview. User-owned references and approved text avoid publisher-content copying and cloud retention by default.

rows.title: No-Spoiler Player Return Brief is a conditional challenger, not a selected product
rows.statement: The buyer hypothesis is a GM/host of a monthly, irregular, open, or paid campaign. Advance only through exact-alternative preference, a non-zero price choice, two three-session pilots, spoiler-safe runtime evidence, rights clearance, and a second-VTT manifest experiment.

rows.title: Campaign-memory payment is real but not an empty market
rows.statement: Archivist publishes campaign-memory plans beginning at $10/month; LegendKeeper publishes a paid owner plan with free player seats; Tavern Scribe explicitly targets missed-session catch-up, player memory, and player truth. This validates a paid category but does not prove a new Return Brief will win.

rows.title: Direct campaign-memory incumbents cover the proposed Return Brief surface
rows.statement: Archivist provides recaps, campaign overviews, private viewer-aware notes, and permission-aware answers; LegendKeeper provides controlled secret content and collaboration; Tavern Scribe provides recap, timeline, character updates, quest progress, and missed-player catch-up.

rows.title: No-Spoiler Player Return Brief is demoted to a comparison arm
rows.statement: Reopen only for a named repeated Foundry-local failure that survives Archivist, Tavern Scribe, LegendKeeper, Campaign Codex, SessionFlow, and the group's manual recap/wiki, followed by a non-zero price choice and a pilot.

rows.title: Module-heavy Foundry tables have high-consequence update and recovery pain
rows.statement: Current community reports describe update breakage, rollback and module-lock workarounds, heavy automation upgrade complexity, and willingness to pay for testing or maintenance support. This recruits qualified GMs but is not product-specific WTP.

rows.title: World Doctor faces a concrete Foundry recovery and compatibility stack
rows.statement: Foundry supplies compatibility warnings, version pinning, package backups, snapshots, migration guidance, and test-install advice; Find the Culprit isolates likely module conflicts; Quick Module Enable filters module sets; Sephral's Content Backup & Restore restores named documents; hosting and duplicate-world practice are additional controls.

rows.title: World Doctor must be a read-only disposable-copy rehearsal and evidence receipt
rows.statement: The candidate launches a GM-selected smoke suite covering join, scene transition, permissions, a representative system roll, journal or macro access, module hooks, and asset resolution, then records observations, unsupported state, and recovery references without mutating the live world or copying campaign content.

rows.title: World Doctor portability is a neutral diagnostic receipt, not cross-VTT runtime parity
rows.statement: A portable artifact may carry package versions, test names, observations, unsupported states, and recovery references without campaign or publisher content. A second VTT begins as a read-only health receipt with visible unsupported mappings.

rows.title: World Doctor is the first empirical buyer gate, not a selected product
rows.statement: Recruit long-running, module-heavy, paid, or tightly scheduled GMs with a named recent incident; test $15/$25/$39/no purchase, exact-alternative preference, two disposable-copy pilots, no-live-mutation runtime evidence, rights/privacy, and a later second-VTT receipt.

rows.title: Current Foundry core closes much of the World Doctor metadata and recovery claim
rows.statement: Foundry exposes compatibility warnings, update and lock controls, package version metadata, backups, snapshots, migration guidance, and test-install advice. A behavioral clone rehearsal would still be distinct, but a compatibility dashboard or backup browser would duplicate current capabilities.

rows.title: Paid hosting already sells parts of the proposed World Doctor workflow
rows.statement: Molten provides a paid second server slot for testing at its Elite tier; VTT Online provides version choice and automated backups; The Forge provides save points. These are exact alternatives for a GM who can rent or duplicate an environment.

rows.title: World Doctor payment evidence remains category evidence rather than product WTP
rows.statement: Paid modules, hosting, maintenance subscriptions, and support indicate Foundry spending, but they do not show that a GM will buy a separate behavioral test runner rather than delay an update, use a backup, or duplicate a world.

rows.title: World Doctor is demoted to a conditional comparison arm
rows.statement: Reopen only for a qualified GM with a named recent breakage or near miss who prefers clone-based behavioral smoke testing over the exact core, hosting, backup, culprit, and duplicate-world workflow, chooses a non-zero price, and pilots on a disposable world.

rows.title: World Doctor portability is a neutral diagnostic receipt
rows.statement: A portable artifact can contain package versions, test names, fingerprints, observations, unsupported states, and recovery references. A second VTT begins as a read-only health receipt; it cannot claim equivalent module or migration runtime.

rows.title: The clearest Foundry payment unit remains prepared content and session value
rows.statement: The official marketplace and premium-content catalog prominently sell ready-made adventures, rules content, maps, tokens, automation, and presentation. Content removes visible preparation and is easier to understand in a listing than an invisible utility.

rows.title: The broad player-economy gap is occupied
rows.statement: Current packages cover system-agnostic shops, D&D5e merchant sheets, reusable shops and traders, buying, selling, crafting, dynamic merchants, post-combat looting, and item trading. A generic loot/shop/inventory product would be a bundle of existing solutions.

rows.title: Attendance-resilient play has a measurable payer segment
rows.statement: Paid and professional GMs can lose booked-session revenue, preparation, and player retention when attendance changes; current Foundry games list per-player and per-session prices. Home groups often cancel, ghost a character, or run a free side adventure, so their pain is a required negative control.

rows.title: Generic drop-in adventure content is already a paid category
rows.statement: Foundry currently lists many paid ready-to-run adventures and interactive premium experiences, while Roll20 allows one-shot and short-adventure listings with a $4.99 minimum. A new product needs a reason beyond more maps, story, or automation.

rows.title: Attendance-Resilient Side Session is a bounded payer test, not a selected product
rows.statement: Test a 60â€“120 minute no-canon capsule that starts with whoever is present, ends cleanly, leaves no hidden state in the main campaign, and produces a safe recap. Advance only if paid/professional or high-variance organizers quantify saved booking or prep value, prefer it over free/adventure/duplicate-world alternatives, choose a non-zero price, and complete two pilots. Continue the wide search in parallel.

rows.title: Battle Replay already covers the broad visual combat-replay claim
rows.statement: Battle Replay records attacks, spells, movement, healing, saves, conditions, and visibility-safe events; it supports synchronized player/GM playback, rewind/seek timelines, cinematic framing, and combat analytics.

rows.title: Current modules cover combat statistics and correction workflows
rows.statement: Combat Stats provides campaign-long damage, healing, kill, accuracy, and ability comparisons; Damage Log provides a visible history with undo/redo; PF2e Combater adds tactical planning and one-click undo.

rows.title: Combat replay and undo interest is real but not product-specific WTP
rows.statement: Community requests ask for replay, rewind, and correction, but common substitutes are screen recording, a system debugger, a damage log, or manual correction. No direct ordinary-table price signal was found for another replay/analytics module.

rows.title: A residual combat-debrief wedge would need player-safe explanations, not another replay
rows.statement: A possible future product could explain visible decisions and rules-review moments without exposing hidden GM information, using a visibility-filtered event envelope, timeline, correction receipt, and export boundary. System semantics and privacy remain high-risk.

rows.title: Generic Combat Replay and Combat Debrief are rejected as new products
rows.statement: Reopen only if a combat-heavy table names a repeated learning or rules-review failure that survives Battle Replay, Combat Stats, Damage Log, PF2e Combater, and native/system tools, then chooses a non-zero price and completes a pilot.

rows.title: Current player-friction pain is real and highly visible
rows.statement: A current PF2e discussion describes players finding Foundry character sheets and combat workflows clunky even after months, with substantial community engagement. This is strong recruiting evidence but not payment evidence.

rows.title: Free current player controls cover most of the generic cockpit claim
rows.statement: Player Pilot provides a free mobile-first control panel; Foundry Navigator provides keyboard-first and screen-reader-friendly navigation; Token Action HUD/PF2e HUD, hidden tabs, tutorials, and the native hotbar cover common action discovery.

rows.title: Current character builders already expose source restrictions and onboarding state
rows.statement: D&D5e Character Builder and D&D Character Creator guide creation and level-up, let GMs select content sources or allowlists, enforce house rules, and show progress or protected drafts. A new character creator or source manager would duplicate the current stack.

rows.title: Player Compass has no direct product-specific WTP after the current stack correction
rows.statement: A read-only automatic context explanation may still reduce repeated â€œwhere do I click?â€ friction, but it must beat the exact system HUD, Navigator, Player Pilot, and character builder stack at a non-zero price and real-table pilot.

rows.title: Retain player accessibility and capability contracts as reusable assets only
rows.statement: Focus recovery, accessible action envelopes, per-user visibility, source policy, and progress receipts may support a future product, but they do not justify a generic player cockpit or mobile panel.

rows.title: Drop-in Dungeons occupies the minimal-preparation emergency-adventure claim
rows.statement: Drop-in Dungeons provides five ready-made 5e dungeon delves with detailed encounters, investigation, dynamic lighting, a bestiary, magic items, and organized navigation. Another generic emergency adventure is not a gap.

rows.title: Paid short-adventure incumbents cover prepared content and multi-system entry
rows.statement: Prepared! 2 provides twelve short adventures for off-plan play, while Dragonshorn Dead Mines is a current multi-system two-to-three-session adventure with imported scenes, linked journals, handouts, maps, tokens, and a $12.95 one-time price.

rows.title: World and table continuity incumbents cover parts of attendance resilience
rows.statement: Omnipresence synchronizes characters, journals, and hotbars across worlds; Oronder provides Discord access, scheduling, downtime, and rewards for West Marches and ordinary campaigns; SessionFlow and cinematic premium adventures cover polished session presentation.

rows.title: Attendance-Resilient Side Session is a no-canon variable-party content-plus-workflow offer
rows.statement: The capsule must run 60â€“120 minutes, start with whoever is present, support current or temporary characters, export only explicit rewards or clues, close cleanly, emit a player-safe recap, and leave no hidden state in the main campaign.

rows.title: The first Attendance-Resilient payer cohort is professional or high-variance organizers
rows.statement: Paid/professional GMs, organized-play coordinators, and West Marches hosts can price lost booking revenue, preparation, or player retention. Home weekly groups often have free social workarounds and are a negative control.

rows.title: Adaptive Drop-In portability requires original content and a neutral manifest
rows.statement: The portable packet can contain original story graph, party-size rules, reward exports, player-safe recap, and unsupported mappings. Foundry is first; Roll20 or Owlbear begins read-only. System-specific stat blocks and art must be original or separately licensed.

rows.title: Attendance-Resilient Side Session remains a bounded first empirical gate, not a selected product
rows.statement: It must beat cancellation, free PDF, premium adventure, duplicate world, Omnipresence, Oronder, and the buyer's current workflow; produce a non-zero price choice, quantify saved booking or preparation value, and complete two pilots. If only professionals pay, report a viable niche and continue the wide search.

rows.title: Per-player audio is a current concrete Foundry pain
rows.statement: A current community request asks for a playlist or boombox that only one player hears and reports that ambient-radius workarounds do not express player identity or level/zone semantics cleanly. This is recruiting evidence, not payment evidence.

rows.title: Foundry playlists are global but recipient-aware audio can be scripted
rows.statement: Core playlists broadcast globally, while the current Foundry audio API can accept explicit recipients. The gap is reliable, discoverable workflow rather than raw runtime impossibility.

rows.title: Current modules occupy pieces of selective audio
rows.statement: Chris Sound Module exposes a specific-player macro but is only verified through Foundry 12; Token Audio FX supports owner-scoped one-shot playback; Enhanced Region Behavior triggers sound/music from regions; Playlist Plus and Narrator's Jukebox occupy general audio control.

rows.title: Audio Secrets is a recipient/scene/queue layer, not another jukebox
rows.statement: The candidate routes user-owned audio to named players, party subsets, token owners, or scene/region conditions; supports queue/loop/private preview; and shows expected recipients without bundling copyrighted music or replacing general playlist management.

rows.title: The strongest payer hypothesis is audio-heavy paid or professional play
rows.statement: Horror, investigation, narrative, actual-play, organized-play, and paid/professional GMs may value private clues and location-specific sound; home weekly groups are a required negative control because macros, voice chat, or headphones may be sufficient.

rows.title: Selective audio has a legible eye-catching demo
rows.statement: â€œThe rogue hears the whisper; the rest of the party hears the roomâ€ demonstrates recipient routing immediately with a live player/zone preview, making the value clearer than a generic audio-settings panel.

rows.title: Selective audio portability requires a neutral route manifest
rows.statement: The portable artifact can contain user-owned asset references, recipient scope, trigger/zone, queue policy, duration, and unsupported fields. Foundry is first; Roll20 or Owlbear begins as a read-only preview.

rows.title: Audio Secrets has no product-specific WTP after the first direct audit
rows.statement: Premium audio packages prove category spending, but routing can be scripted and current modules cover pieces. Advance only after a named repeated incident, exact-alternative rejection, a non-zero one-time price, two pilots, and privacy/rights/runtime proof.

rows.title: Current Foundry audio packages occupy generic soundscape automation
rows.statement: Soundscape Adventure is current through Foundry 14 and provides a cross-world sound library, moods, random/sequential loops, intensity, and triggers from regions, combats, and scenes.

rows.title: Roll20 already occupies the generic playlist control surface
rows.statement: Roll20 provides a global Jukebox and its Jukebox Plus documentation covers playlists, albums, looping, previews, styled feedback, and backup handouts.

rows.title: Owlbear portability is an extension package, not runtime parity
rows.statement: Owlbear Rodeo supports manifest-loaded extensions, popovers, tools, and custom context menus, but a portable audio product would need its own extension and cannot assume a shared audio engine.

rows.title: The portable audio boundary is intent metadata only
rows.statement: A neutral route manifest can preserve user-owned asset references, recipient scope, trigger, queue, duration, reward/clue linkage, and unsupported fields; it cannot guarantee equivalent playback, hosting, auth, or permission semantics.

rows.title: Generic Audio Secrets is too crowded for first implementation
rows.statement: Foundry Soundscape Adventure, Roll20 Jukebox/Jukebox Plus, recipient macros, Token Audio FX, Whisper As, and Owlbear extensions make a broad cross-VTT audio utility expensive to differentiate and maintain.

rows.title: Premium content provides a direct payment path
rows.statement: Foundry's premium-content and publisher guidance explicitly supports paid assets, adventures, audio packs, content keys, Patreon access, and one-time or recurring publisher delivery.

rows.title: Existing modules cover private delivery components
rows.statement: Whisper As supports selected recipients and in-character aliases; Louder Whispers makes private messages noticeable; Soundscape Adventure covers ambient organization and triggers.

rows.title: Whisper Drop-In combines original content with asymmetric delivery
rows.statement: The provisional product is a 60â€“120 minute, no-canon variable-party scenario with private audio clues, clean resolution, explicit reward/clue export, player-safe recap, and no hidden writes to the main campaign.

rows.title: Whisper Drop-In has a clearer payer than a generic audio utility
rows.statement: Paid/professional GMs, organized-play and rotating-party hosts, and horror/investigation GMs can value a ready-to-run fallback and an immediately visible asymmetric clue mechanic; home groups remain a negative control.

rows.title: Whisper Drop-In is the strongest new hypothesis but remains unvalidated
rows.statement: Advance only if qualified buyers prefer it over cancellation, free PDF, premium adventure, Drop-in Dungeons, Oronder, Soundscape plus Whisper As, generic audio packs, and manual play; choose a non-zero price and complete pilots with rights/runtime/portability proof.

rows.title: World-clock resource reminders are a repeated community request
rows.statement: A community request asks for timers keyed to in-game world time for wandering-monster checks and torch burn-out rather than real seconds.

rows.title: System-agnostic torch burn-down is an explicit request
rows.statement: A separate request asks for a Shadowdark-style torch timer that consumes inventory, shows time remaining, and can announce a flavorful burn-out message for 5e or other systems.

rows.title: Expedition Tracker occupies basic expedition turns and timed effects
rows.statement: Expedition Tracker supports dungeon and overland turns, optional wandering-monster rolls, and timed effects that can apply and remove light sources.

rows.title: Light Sources occupies inventory-backed torch burn-down
rows.statement: Light Sources is current through Foundry 14 and provides one-click inventory-backed lighting, in-game or real-time durations, automatic burn-out, chat notices, and multiple light patterns.

rows.title: Campaign pressure and timer packages close the broad resource surface
rows.statement: Party Operations covers watches, marching order, torchlight, supplies, readiness, and campaign pressure; SessionFlow covers travel watches, supply/fatigue, progress clocks, and broadcast state; Flip Timer covers shared countdowns.

rows.title: Resource interest is not new-product WTP
rows.statement: Community requests and category coverage establish a real problem but do not show that buyers will pay for another generic timer, resource ledger, or expedition dashboard.

rows.title: Accessibility failure is a recurring Foundry concern
rows.statement: A feature discussion reports poor screen-reader and keyboard-only accessibility, and community reports describe difficulty making Foundry text and controls usable for vision-impaired players.

rows.title: Foundry Navigator is a current D&D5e accessibility incumbent
rows.statement: Foundry Navigator supports Foundry v13/v14 D&D5e keyboard-first and screen-reader workflows across sheets, combat, token movement, announcements, low resolution, and focus recovery, while acknowledging incomplete support.

rows.title: Accessibility Enhancements is an older PF2e-oriented incumbent
rows.statement: Accessibility Enhancements provides drag-and-drop alternatives, audio feedback, and high-contrast PF2e sheets, but its latest verified version is through Foundry 12.

rows.title: Accessible Table Kit must remain a player-local accessibility layer
rows.statement: The candidate should provide semantic navigation, announcements, focus recovery, low-resolution layout, token/scene lists, and native-sheet escape hatches without copying rules or becoming a new automation engine.

rows.title: Accessibility has a qualified payer segment but is not broad by default
rows.statement: Likely payers are GMs with a named disabled player, paid GMs, schools/libraries, organized-play hosts, and accessibility-conscious communities; ordinary home tables with no incident are a negative control.

rows.title: Accessibility portability is semantic-contract portability
rows.statement: Keyboard commands, announcements, focus targets, preferences, and unsupported controls can be described neutrally, but Foundry, Roll20, and Owlbear do not share a common accessibility runtime.

rows.title: Accessibility support carries a large maintenance matrix
rows.statement: A commercial accessibility layer would need a bounded supported matrix across system sheets, browsers, screen readers, third-party modules, and changing Foundry markup; every unsupported path can become a support incident.

rows.title: Accessible Table Kit requires specialist buyer validation
rows.statement: The product must beat Foundry Navigator, Accessibility Enhancements, native OS tools, custom CSS, and the exact system sheet on a named failure before a price claim is credible.

rows.title: Accessible Table Kit is the strongest fresh need but remains unselected
rows.statement: Accessibility has clearer human need and less generic saturation than resource timers, but it is not selected until qualified buyers choose a non-zero price, complete pilots, and accept the bounded scope.

rows.title: Dungeon Master's Forge remains backburnered
rows.statement: The fresh research must not reopen or modify Dungeon Master's Forge; its assets may be reconsidered only after a separate product passes the market gates.

rows.title: General Foundry cognitive-load pain is real but heterogeneous
rows.statement: A current PF2e discussion reports players repeatedly losing time in a complex character sheet with too many tabs, while other users describe tab management, HUDs, and system learning as sufficient remedies.

rows.title: Player Pilot occupies simplified player control
rows.statement: Player Pilot provides a mobile-first player control panel for common actor actions, spells, features, movement, targeting, pings, rests, and requests without requiring the full character sheet.

rows.title: HUD and UI-overhaul products occupy broad player simplification
rows.statement: Foundry Navigator, Stylish Action HUD, Carolingian UI, SessionFlow, and system-specific HUD/configuration workflows cover substantial keyboard, action, presentation, focus, and clutter-reduction needs.

rows.title: Broad Cognitive Access is not a differentiated product
rows.statement: The broad promise of a simpler Foundry experience mixes onboarding, system complexity, accessibility, HUD preference, and personal configuration; current alternatives make a new paid utility difficult to distinguish.

rows.title: Semantic focus and action contracts remain reusable
rows.statement: Focus targets, announcements, keyboard commands, and player-action intents can be retained as neutral assets even though each VTT and system implements them differently.

rows.title: Post-import false-green failures are concrete
rows.statement: A community report describes scenes, journals, actors, and sounds importing while journal links remain unreferenced, including internal links, even in a blank test world.

rows.title: VTT migration has no common formal portability standard
rows.statement: A current migration discussion reports that D&D Beyond and Roll20 lack a formal common export/import path, Roll20 export is constrained, Foundry formats change, and converters are best effort.

rows.title: DDB-Importer already covers substantial D&D5e adventure import
rows.statement: Current DDB-Importer supports Foundry 14 and imports many D&D Beyond adventures with walls, lighting, journals, and monsters, alongside characters, items, encounters, maps, and other content.

rows.title: Migration Safe Harbor is a post-import assurance receipt
rows.statement: The candidate is a local, read-only, disposable-copy pass that checks links, assets, scene geometry, permissions, duplicates, overwrites, compatibility, unsupported fields, and play-tonight smoke conditions.

rows.title: Migration Safe Harbor has a clearer but episodic GM payer
rows.statement: Active migrating GMs, long-running campaign owners, paid GMs, and small publishers may pay to reduce migration deadline and game-night risk; ordinary players are not the payer.

rows.title: Foundry-native packaging and repair tools close much of the assurance claim
rows.statement: Foundry Adventure Documents preserve internal links for Foundry imports; Scene Packer supplies an asset report; Asset Auditor finds missing paths; Lore Reference Board performs import-time link checks and relinking; RPGNautas advertises deep link repair.

rows.title: The residual migration wedge is a named false-green, not migration in general
rows.statement: A new product must find a failure that remains after the exact source importer and current repair tools complete; otherwise manual cleanup or free modules rationally win.

rows.title: Migration Safe Harbor must not scrape or proxy source accounts
rows.statement: Roll20/D&D Beyond credentials, unsupported scraping, publisher-content retention, or license circumvention would create unacceptable platform and rights risk.

rows.title: The portable BridgeCheck artifact is a receipt, not a converter
rows.statement: A neutral receipt can contain IDs, document kinds, asset fingerprints, link states, package versions, permission scopes, check results, repair proposals, and unsupported states; runtime mutation remains VTT-specific.

rows.title: Migration Safe Harbor is stronger than resource or broad accessibility on payment intent
rows.statement: Migration deadlines and paid importers provide a clearer GM payment proxy than generic resource timers or general UI/accessibility interest, but this is category evidence and the use is episodic.

rows.title: Migration Safe Harbor remains unselected
rows.statement: Promote only after qualified migrating GMs prefer the receipt over exact importer-plus-cleanup, choose a non-zero price, complete disposable-copy pilots, and accept the credential/content boundary.

rows.title: DDB-Importer has a current paid-access and maintenance boundary
rows.statement: DDB-Importer is current through Foundry 14 and documents Patreon or user-run proxy access for some monster, adventure, sync, and support features, while maintaining multiple Foundry/D&D5e version lines.

rows.title: Active GMs pay for import capability when value is concrete
rows.statement: Current importer access and historical community discussions provide a category payment proxy for active GMs who value retained content, saved preparation, and ongoing compatibility.

rows.title: Importer payment does not prove receipt payment
rows.statement: An importer produces or transforms content, while Migration Safe Harbor only diagnoses uncertainty after import; category WTP cannot be transferred without a decision-changing false-green result.

rows.title: Post-update regression checks may create repeat value
rows.statement: A buyer may have a second payment reason if a Foundry, system, or module update can silently invalidate a previously trusted imported campaign.

rows.title: Package warnings and manual clone tests are controls for regression assurance
rows.statement: Foundry package/version warnings, importer support paths, backups, and a manual disposable clone can detect or contain some post-update failures.

rows.title: Payment validation must exclude proxy and credential handling
rows.statement: Importer proxy access may require source-account credentials, but Migration Safe Harbor must inspect only user-owned output and must not collect cookies, operate a proxy, scrape, or retain publisher content.

rows.title: Paid-session attendance has direct economic consequences
rows.statement: StartPlaying charges players per session, charges signed-up no-shows, and does not charge when the GM cancels; this makes seat utilization and session continuity a concrete paid-GM concern.

rows.title: Attendance policy is already owned by booking platforms
rows.statement: StartPlaying provides skip windows, charges, refunds, price waivers, player removal, and no-show guidance, while Warhorn provides event registration, schedules, table planning, and payments.

rows.title: Qualified attendance buyers are paid and organized-play operators
rows.statement: Paid/professional GMs, organized-play hosts, and event organizers have revenue, seat, and reputation consequences that ordinary home tables often avoid by postponing.

rows.title: Attendance pain does not justify a new roster module
rows.statement: The money signal validates a payer segment but not a new scheduler, roster, or cancellation tool because incumbents already perform those jobs.

rows.title: The residual job is preserving value when party size changes
rows.statement: The unmet hypothesis is keeping a paid or high-value session worthwhile when one or more expected players disappear, not tracking attendance itself.

rows.title: SessionFlow occupies broad Foundry session orchestration
rows.statement: SessionFlow provides beat and scene sequencing, quick scenes, progress clocks, player widgets, recaps, and a player-facing canvas, weakening a generic session-dashboard pitch.

rows.title: Scene Packer and drop-in content lower emergency-prep cost
rows.statement: Scene Packer preserves links and assets across imported scenes, while existing drop-in products already sell minimal-preparation adventures.

rows.title: Attendance Rescue must be content-shaped
rows.statement: A defensible wedge is a bounded no-canon side session with variable-party entry, an explicit exit, and campaign-safe reward or recap export rather than another attendance control panel.

rows.title: Table Rescue is a conditional candidate
rows.statement: The product may preserve a valuable session for paid/professional or rotating-party GMs, but generic one-shot content and current emergency workflows remain strong alternatives.

rows.title: The portable product is a neutral scenario package
rows.statement: A PDF plus scenario, branch, reward, and recap manifest can be run manually in Foundry, Roll20, Owlbear, or theater of the mind without an account bridge.

rows.title: Table Rescue targets paid and high-variance tables
rows.statement: The primary buyer is a paid/professional GM, organized-play host, or rotating-party organizer; an ordinary home group that can postpone is a negative control.

rows.title: The eye-catching promise is one-click party-size recovery
rows.statement: A demo that switches to a two-player branch and exports a clean campaign-safe handoff is more legible than attendance management, but visual appeal cannot substitute for price choice or pilot evidence.

rows.title: Table Rescue must beat exact emergency alternatives
rows.statement: The buyer comparison must include cancellation/refund, running short, improvising, a free one-shot, premium adventures, Drop-in Dungeons, Oronder, SessionFlow, and the GMâ€™s own emergency folder.

rows.title: Table Rescue can avoid live campaign mutation
rows.statement: A disposable Foundry package can keep branches, hidden/public clue scope, rewards, and recap export isolated from the main world until the GM explicitly imports a result.

rows.title: Table Rescue remains unselected pending buyer evidence
rows.statement: The product needs qualified preference, non-zero price, two real pilots, and a home-table negative control before implementation.

rows.title: Table Rescue should use original or licensed assets
rows.statement: A portable rescue scenario must not copy publisher adventures, depend on source credentials, or require a hosted account bridge.

rows.title: Players can be connected but unable to play
rows.statement: Community reports describe players losing token movement, scene visibility, actor visibility, or interaction until refresh/reconnect, creating repeated session disruption.

rows.title: Foundry reliability failures have multiple root causes
rows.statement: Foundry identifies module conflicts, oversized images, hardware acceleration, missing assets, disk space, and network conditions as different scene-loading causes.

rows.title: Paid and high-investment tables have a stronger reliability consequence
rows.statement: A paid GM, organized host, or long-running campaign owner loses session time, money, reputation, or player trust when a table must restart.

rows.title: A Foundry module cannot promise universal network repair
rows.statement: Router, ISP, browser, GPU, hosting, and arbitrary module-conflict causes are not all observable or fixable from a local add-on.

rows.title: Session Continuity should measure safe continuation
rows.statement: The defensible job is distinguishing connected, interactive, scene-ready, and current clients, then exposing an explicit recovery path.

rows.title: Connection Monitor already covers basic disconnect state
rows.statement: Connection Monitor detects disconnections/reconnections and visually disables or de-emphasizes controls while disconnected, but does not prove scene readiness or recover uncertain actions.

rows.title: Performance Optimizer covers client rendering health
rows.statement: Performance Optimizer provides per-player profiles, low-FPS detection, GM controls, and a benchmark/live FPS view, so a generic performance panel is occupied.

rows.title: Core Foundry covers several preload and recovery controls
rows.statement: Core provides scene preload, safe configuration, package backups, and snapshots, so Session Continuity must not repackage those controls without decision-changing evidence.

rows.title: Generic connection and hosting products are rejected
rows.statement: Hosting, browser/GPU fixes, network repair, and general connection banners are exact alternatives or outside the module boundary.

rows.title: The residual wedge is a reliability receipt and recovery workflow
rows.statement: The gap is an evidence-linked â€œsafe to continue / waiting / unknownâ€ answer with scene identity, readiness signals, last confirmed event, and explicit pending action.

rows.title: Session Continuity is a conditional recurring-pain candidate
rows.statement: A client-health and safe-rejoin layer could serve paid or high-investment tables, but existing controls and hosting remain strong alternatives.

rows.title: Safe rejoin must not replay uncertain actions
rows.statement: A disconnected or stale client may have submitted, partially submitted, or never submitted an action; recovery must preserve uncertainty rather than guess or mutate the world.

rows.title: The portable artifact is a neutral health/recovery receipt
rows.statement: A receipt can carry client/session/scene identity, readiness, last confirmed server event, pending/unknown action, and unsupported state without sharing player content or requiring a hosted bridge.

rows.title: The eye-catching demo is proof of who can safely continue
rows.statement: A GM sees exactly which player is interactive and ready while a reconnecting player receives a clear scene and unsent-action status; the demo is legible without claiming network repair.

rows.title: Session Continuity must beat exact controls
rows.statement: The buyer comparison includes Connection Monitor, Performance Optimizer, core preload/safe mode, backups, hosting support, browser/GPU fixes, and refreshing.

rows.title: Session Continuity remains unselected pending pilots
rows.statement: Qualified preference, non-zero price, multi-session pilots, and a home-table negative control are required before implementation.

rows.title: Session Continuity can avoid content and credential collection
rows.statement: A health/recovery receipt can be generated from local/session metadata without uploading player content, collecting credentials, or operating a hosted service.
